This person is a 42-year-old owner of a 20-employee precision engineering SME in Coventry exporting most components to Germany and France; they want the UK to prioritize re-entry to the customs union and single market for goods, remove rules of origin, re-align product standards to CE marking to avoid duplicate UKCA testing, and integrate fully with EU transit and customs IT so just-in-time deliveries stop missing slots; they care because border friction since 2021 forced them to hold costly buffer stock and they lost an Italian client over certification delays. Duplicate UKCA and CE conformity tests on the same components now cost them about £30,000 a year and add 3–4 weeks to each new part release, so mutual recognition of standards is their top priority. Last spring, a just-in-time shipment to a German tier‑one client missed its slot after a GVMS outage at Dover, triggering a €7,500 chargeback and a “supplier at risk” flag on their scorecard. Carrying six weeks of buffer stock now ties up about £250,000 in working capital that they say could otherwise fund a new 5‑axis mill and two apprentices. They stress that a customs union alone wouldn’t solve their biggest pain—duplicate UKCA/CE conformity assessment—unless the UK also recognises CE marking and aligns product standards.

This person is a 55-year-old CEO of a Leeds-based medical device manufacturer that invested heavily in UKCA-only labeling and MHRA approvals; they oppose a rapid rejoin unless there is a multi-year grandfathering period for UKCA certificates, reciprocal acceptance of MHRA-assessed clinical evidence under EU MDR, and grant support for relabeling lines; they care because they spent £1.2m retooling for UKCA and a sudden switch back to CE would strand inventory and invalidate packaging artwork already printed. After an MHRA labeling guidance tweak in 2023, they had to pulp 20,000 pre-printed UKCA cartons and redo artwork at a £60k loss, making them unwilling to back rejoin without firm grandfathering and relabeling support. We still hold £300k of UKCA‑labelled finished goods that would become unsellable overnight without multi‑year grandfathering and help to relabel. In 2022 our attempt to secure an EU MDR Notified Body slot was pushed to late 2025 at roughly triple the cost of our UK Approved Body, which is why we committed fully to UKCA. Because our EU MDR Notified Body slot isn’t until late 2025, a rejoin without at least a three-year UKCA certificate grandfathering would force a sales gap and potential staff furloughs.

This person is the HR director of an NHS trust in Cornwall facing double-digit nurse vacancy rates; they want early restoration of freedom of movement for health occupations, automatic mutual recognition of nursing and midwifery qualifications, a temporary bridging visa for EEA clinicians during the accession period, and removal of the immigration health surcharge for NHS recruits; they care because agency spend is unsustainable and current salary thresholds and visa fees are blocking hires. Last winter we had to cancel elective lists after three Portuguese and two Spanish nurses withdrew when salary thresholds, visa fees and NMC recognition delays derailed their start dates. They calculate that exempting NHS recruits from the immigration health surcharge would save their trust about £120,000 this year. The make-or-break for us is automatic mutual recognition of EU nursing qualifications, which would let me confirm start dates in four weeks instead of three months. Last quarter we lost four EU theatre nurses to hospitals in Ireland because their qualifications were recognised automatically and there were no visa fees, while ours took three months.

This person is a Border Force union representative at Dover; they want any rejoin policy to retain UK non-participation in Schengen and full control over visa policy, with negotiated protocols that preserve UK primary border checks and clear investment in exit/entry systems integration without accepting Schengen acquis obligations; they care because staffing, rostering, and infrastructure are built around current controls and abrupt changes could compromise security and working conditions. After we tested the French EES biometric kiosks at Dover and coach turnarounds spiked, I concluded we need UK‑controlled queueing and staffing guarantees baked into any rejoin deal. I was the duty manager during the bank‑holiday EES pilot when coach processing times doubled and we had to cancel staff leave to keep lanes open. During the EES pilot I filed incident reports for staff fatigue and coach gridlock, so I want UK‑set lane allocation and surge staffing written into any rejoin protocol. I handled three post-pilot grievances for injuries and stress, so I want legally binding surge-staffing triggers in any protocol.

This person is a 34-year-old UK citizen in Birmingham married to a Polish architect on pre-settled status; they want early adoption of EU free movement provisions, no-fee conversion of settled and pre-settled statuses to EU residence rights, and restoration of mutual recognition of professional qualifications so the spouse can work on EU projects without duplicative licensing; they care because visa renewal anxiety and lost work opportunities in Germany have delayed buying a home and starting their own firm. We lost a Berlin project when my spouse was told to re-qualify and pay for fresh translations despite already being licensed in Poland, so early automatic recognition is our top priority. We want a legally binding commitment to immediate alignment with the EU Professional Qualifications Directive so my spouse’s Polish license is recognized across the EU from day one. If recognition is phased in rather than immediate, she still won’t be able to sign as project architect in Germany next year, forcing us to skip another round of EU tenders. The Berlin Architektenkammer told us Anerkennung would take 9–12 months and cost a few thousand euros, effectively blocking her from next year’s EU tenders.

This person is a 68-year-old sovereignty campaigner in Hartlepool who canvassed for Brexit; they will only accept any rejoin process that includes a national referendum, explicit parliamentary safeguards against automatic supremacy of EU law, and firm political assurances that the UK will not be obliged to adopt the euro or join Schengen; they care because they believe border control, lawmaking, and trade policy should remain fully accountable to Westminster voters. His brother's trawler was repeatedly idled by EU quota limits, cementing his view that fisheries policy must be decided in Westminster. Having lost seasonal income crewing on his brother’s boat when EU quotas kept them in port, he insists any rejoin deal leave Westminster in charge of fisheries quotas and access. If rejoining put the UK back under the Common Fisheries Policy, he says he'd lose the winter crewing money that tops up his pension when haddock and cod quotas tighten. He wants any rejoin deal to guarantee UK control of the 12-mile limit and foreign vessel licensing to protect small crews like his brother’s.

This person is a 49-year-old trawler skipper from Peterhead landing cod and haddock; they oppose rejoining unless the UK secures improved quota shares under the Common Fisheries Policy, tight joint enforcement against foreign incursions in UK waters, and a multi-year compensation and fleet modernisation fund to manage any quota cuts; they care because their margins depend on allocations and they fear a return to what they view as unfair relative stability keys. He still remembers tying up for a fortnight in 2014 when his cod quota closed early, forcing him to lay off two crew. He wants quotas recalculated on zonal attachment because his North Sea grounds now hold more cod than when the old relative stability shares were set. He leases in cod quota each year at steep prices, and says reverting to EU relative stability would spike lease costs and wipe out his margin. Last summer a foreign netter cut through his gear off Rattray Head, cementing his demand for joint patrols with real penalties for incursions.

This person is a marine conservation scientist at an NGO in Brighton; they support rejoining to align with CFP ecosystem-based management, binding maximum sustainable yield targets, and joint control regimes, and want the UK to champion closed spawning areas, stronger bycatch rules, and transparent data sharing in EU councils; they care because fragmented post-Brexit governance has complicated stock assessments and undermined North Sea recovery plans. Last year I had to suspend our North Sea cod bycatch project when loss of joint EU–UK observer and survey data left our models blind to half the fleet. If rejoining restores shared VMS/ERS access under the EU Data Collection Framework, my team can relaunch the cod bycatch models within months. If the UK rejoined but negotiated derogations from CFP data-sharing and joint control, our cod bycatch risk models would remain blind to half the trawl effort. Our next grant milestone requires publishing updated cod bycatch risk maps by autumn, which we can't meet without restored EU VMS/ERS feeds and joint observer datasets.

This person is a 37-year-old arable farmer in Cambridgeshire whose basic payments declined under new domestic schemes; they want rejoining to reintroduce predictable CAP direct payments with eco-schemes compatible with their crop rotations, phased SPS alignment to smooth grain exports to EU buyers, and credit for recent environmental investments during the transition; they care because bank financing hinges on stable income streams and reliable market access. Last season a barley shipment to Belgium was held five days for SPS checks, forcing a £10/tonne discount that strained their cashflow. Their Belgian maltster has told them full SPS alignment would lift the £10/t risk discount currently applied to their forward barley contracts. My bank manager has warned my overdraft will be cut next season unless I can show predictable support payments or SPS-aligned contracts with EU buyers. If re-entry phased in SPS alignment but delayed CAP-style direct payments, I’d still face a cashflow gap my bank says it won’t finance.

This person is a low-income consumer advocate in Tower Hamlets working with food banks; they worry that rejoining without safeguards could raise food prices via CAP protections and constrain UK flexibility on VAT relief, so they want the UK to push for CAP reform toward targeted environmental payments, secure the ability to keep zero VAT on essentials within EU VAT rules, and fund targeted rebates for vulnerable households; they care because small price increases cascade into hunger for the people they support. They are especially worried about losing the UK's zero VAT on children's clothes and school shoes, which would squeeze parents at uniform-buying time. I run the back-to-school voucher fund at our food bank, so if rejoining meant losing the zero VAT on children’s clothes, our entire uniform budget would evaporate. I’ve costed it: losing zero VAT on kids’ clothes would add about £12 to a £60 uniform kit, wiping out a third of each voucher we issue. I’d only support rejoining if the accession treaty hardwires a derogation preserving zero VAT on children’s clothes and school shoes.

This person is a 42-year-old Midlands precision-engineering SME owner employing 75 people who exports 65% of turnover to Germany and the Netherlands; they want re-accession implemented with immediate re-entry to the Single Market and Customs Union, reinstatement of CE-marking acceptance and mutual recognition of conformity assessment, HMRC-funded vouchers for re-testing to EU standards, simplified CDS/GVMS processes and AEO fast-track for SMEs, and a 12-18 month transition where UKCA and CE markings are both valid to prevent scrapping inventory. We wrote off £120,000 last year when a German client rejected a batch because a UK-accredited lab’s certificate wasn’t EU-recognized post-Brexit, so mutual recognition of conformity assessment is my top priority. Without mutual recognition of conformity assessment, our German clients require EU‑lab retesting that adds six weeks to delivery and triggers costly late‑delivery penalties. If re-entry is phased without immediate MRCA, we'd likely cut eight to ten jobs to absorb retesting delays and penalties. I personally flew parts to Eindhoven for EU-lab retesting last quarter, spending £3,100 and still missing the client's penalty window by two days.

This person is a 58-year-old inshore fishing skipper from Newlyn, Cornwall whose income improved with post-Brexit quota gains; they will oppose rejoining unless the negotiating mandate secures multi-year derogations under the Common Fisheries Policy for small-scale fleets, legally binding minimum national quota shares above 2015 baselines, ring-fenced EMFAF-style support for gear changes and port infrastructure, and community co-management councils written into the accession treaty before Parliament ratifies. He still remembers tying up his 9.8‑metre boat in July when the under‑10m pool quota ran out while French and Spanish boats worked just outside 12 miles. He is still repaying a five-year loan for a chilled hold and net hauler bought after the post‑Brexit quota boost, and fears he’ll default if quota shares revert to relative‑stability baselines. Without ring‑fenced EMFAF‑style grants, he can’t afford the selective gear and quay‑side ice hookup his buyer now requires for winter cuttlefish and mackerel landings. He’s calculated that reverting to 2015 relative‑stability shares would cut his mackerel and cuttlefish landings by a third, pushing his loan into arrears.

This person is a 46-year-old NHS hospital HR director in Greater Manchester responsible for staffing 900 nurses; they want the implementation plan to front-load mutual recognition of professional qualifications under Directive 2005/36/EC, a joint NMC/GMC-EU fast-track desk to clear backlogs within 90 days, temporary bridging visas during the transition, immediate association to Erasmus+ to rebuild training pipelines, and portable pension and indemnity arrangements so EU clinicians can start safely on day one. Last winter I had to keep 12 surgical beds closed for six weeks because a cohort of EU nurses were stuck in NMC recognition limbo and couldn't start. We lost eight EU nurses to Ireland and Germany last year after NMC recognition dragged past five months, forcing me to cover gaps with costly agency shifts. Restoring Erasmus+ would let me reopen our Manchester–Valencia placement pipeline that supplied 15 nurses a year pre-Brexit. Our workforce modelling shows that each month NMC recognition drags adds roughly £200,000 in agency costs and forces us to cancel planned theatre lists.

This person is a 29-year-old warehouse operative in Ashford, Kent on a zero-hours contract worried about wage undercutting and housing pressure; they insist the accession treaty include a time-limited safeguard clause that can temporarily restrict free movement if local unemployment or vacancy rates trigger thresholds, guaranteed funding to restore a Migration Impact Fund for councils, beefed-up HMRC enforcement against minimum wage abuses, and ring-fenced apprenticeships so any labour inflow is matched by skills investment. I was once paid below the minimum wage after agency deductions, so tougher HMRC enforcement is the part I care about most. After my temp agency folded and dodged my arrears, I want HMRC to carry out unannounced warehouse inspections and hold host employers jointly liable for minimum wage breaches. I never recovered the £650 I was owed when the agency folded, so making host warehouses jointly liable for minimum wage breaches is non-negotiable for me. If joint liability is included, I’d finally feel safe taking agency shifts; without it, I avoid them even when hours dry up.

This person is a 50-year-old operations manager at an agri-food processor in County Armagh, Northern Ireland juggling dual-regime paperwork; they want rejoining sequenced to remove Irish Sea checks by moving to a single UK-EU SPS and customs regime, a published timeline for when Windsor Framework easements sunset, expanded trusted-trader and green-lane schemes during the transition, and a one-stop helpline that clarifies when EU customs code will apply uniformly across GB and NI. I spend 12 hours a week reconciling dual TARIC/UKGT codes and chasing TRACES/IPAFFS entries to stop loads being held at Larne. Last quarter a TRACES/IPAFFS mismatch held £30k of fresh poultry at Larne for 48 hours, forcing us to bin the load—full SPS alignment would have avoided it. A fixed cutover to TRACES-only across GB and NI would immediately save me 10+ hours a week and prevent the IPAFFS/TRACES mismatches that keep holding our loads. What I need most is a hard TRACES-only go-live date so I can retrain our three coordinators and switch off duplicate IPAFFS processes.

This person is a 39-year-old CFO of a Speyside whisky distillery exporting heavily to the US and Asia; they back rejoining only if the government simultaneously preserves continuity of post-Brexit FTAs by negotiating rollover clauses and cumulation fixes for rules of origin, secures tariff-rate quota access at least equal to current schedules, protects Scotch whisky geographical indications in both EU and non-EU markets, and publishes a legal instrument that prevents a cliff-edge loss of CPTPP and UK-Japan preferences during the EU accession transition. Last year we spent over £60,000 fighting a “Scotch‑style” knock‑off in Vietnam, so enforceable GI protection in both EU and non‑EU markets is my red line. We have £8m of forward contracts in Japan and Vietnam priced on CEPA/CPTPP zero-tariff access, so any EU rejoin pathway that risks a lapse in those preferences would blow our margins. In 2021 a paperwork gap meant one Vietnam shipment cleared at MFN, costing us £38,000 and a lost listing—I’m not risking a repeat during accession. Our bank covenants require me to certify uninterrupted CEPA/CPTPP preferential access 90 days before shipment, so without a statutory continuity backstop we'd have to halt Japan and Vietnam orders during accession.

This person is a 37-year-old Home Office caseworker in Sheffield who processes EU Settlement Scheme applications; they want a staged plan that preserves Withdrawal Agreement rights while reintroducing free movement, including legislation to merge or sunset EUSS without creating gaps in right-to-work and right-to-rent checks, investment to upgrade the Atlas caseworking IT and expand UKVCAS appointments, automatic conversion of pre-settled to settled status where eligible, a single digital status portal interoperable with DWP and HMRC, and clear guidance on ECJ jurisdiction over citizens' rights to avoid judicial review risk. After an Atlas outage caused right-to-work mismatches and a flurry of pre-action letters, they became fixated on real-time, interoperable status checks before any rejoin move. Their Portuguese spouse briefly lost a job offer when a right-to-work check failed during an Atlas lag, cementing their push for real-time, interoperable status verification. A right-to-rent mismatch last year nearly cost them and their Portuguese spouse their flat, so they want interoperable landlord checks in place before any EUSS sunset. They’ve volunteered for UAT of a real-time status checker with DWP and HMRC so employers and landlords can verify rights instantly during any EUSS sunset.

This person is a 62-year-old retired Army veteran in Lincolnshire who campaigned for sovereignty; if rejoining proceeds, they demand a legally binding referendum on the final accession treaty, retention of non-Schengen status and a formal euro opt-out protocol, selective opt-outs from Justice and Home Affairs akin to Denmark's, a parliamentary scrutiny reserve that requires Commons approval before ministers agree to new EU measures, and domestic legislation clarifying the limits of ECJ jurisdiction over UK criminal law. A few years ago his son was detained in Spain under a European Arrest Warrant with minimal UK judicial scrutiny, cementing his insistence on tight limits to ECJ authority over criminal law. Because his Armed Forces pension and savings are in sterling, he sees any pressure to adopt the euro as a direct risk to his finances. His brother runs a small arable farm near Boston, so he fears CAP rules returning would complicate planting and subsidy choices. After helping his brother navigate the new SFI applications, he dreads CAP's cross-compliance and greening rules returning to tie up the farm in paperwork.

This person is a 27-year-old tenant sheep and arable farmer in North Yorkshire on a tight margin; they want entry to the Common Agricultural Policy designed to avoid cash-flow gaps by phasing Basic Income Support while integrating England's ELM eco-schemes, a small-farm redistributive top-up, continuity in cross-compliance/conditionality so inspections are predictable, DEFRA-funded advisory support to navigate CAP IT systems, and interoperability of livestock movement data with TRACES so animals can move seamlessly to EU markets. Last autumn I lost money on store lambs after TRACES mismatches delayed export for weeks, so interoperable movement data is my top priority. If ARAMS data synced automatically with TRACES NT for EHCs, I could restart store lamb exports without tying up cash for weeks. As a tenant, those export delays pushed me over my overdraft, nearly missing rent and risking the tenancy. Last year I spent 10 days shuttling between my vet, APHA and the haulier to reconcile ARAMS–TRACES NT data, missed my ferry slot, and wiped out the small rent buffer I rely on.

This person is a 48-year-old chartered accountant in Surrey active in a taxpayer advocacy group; they want the government to publish an itemised, OBR-scored forecast of gross and net EU budget contributions over 10 years, a negotiating objective for a rebate or contribution cap, a transparent dashboard comparing UK CAP receipts and structural funds to contributions by region, and a fiscal rule that any additional EU payments are offset by identified savings or tax measures, with NAO auditing of all transition costs. Having audited a Surrey LEP project part-funded by EU structural funds and uncovering opaque cost overruns, they now insist any rejoin transition is NAO-audited. He once arranged an emergency overdraft for a Surrey manufacturing client when an EU structural fund reimbursement arrived months late, so he now insists on enforceable payment timetables in any rejoin transition. He wants the OBR to publish exchange‑rate and inflation sensitivities for euro‑denominated contributions to prevent mid‑year cashflow shocks to UK budgets. He would only support rejoin if euro‑denominated contributions are hedged with a clear, NAO‑monitored FX policy to prevent budget shocks.

This person is a 57-year-old care home owner in Cornwall who has struggled to fill vacancies since 2021 and wants any application to rejoin the EU to front-load labour mobility: they argue the government should file under Article 49 while simultaneously negotiating an interim mobility chapter targeted at health and social care, fast-track mutual recognition of nursing and care qualifications, and re-align with EU rules on professional credentials so their EU staff can be onboarded without months-long visa and verification delays. Last year they kept eight beds empty for two months because two experienced Polish carers were held up by visa and qualification checks. I’ve postponed opening a new dementia wing because I can’t recruit without faster EU credential recognition. My priority is a 60-day provisional practice permit for EU-qualified carers so they can start under supervision while full visa and credential checks complete. A 60-day supervised permit would have let me open the dementia wing on time and hire 10 local support workers alongside EU carers.

This person is a 45-year-old Home Office border security policy lead in London who would only support rejoining if implementation is phased to protect border integrity: they want a clear timetable for reintroducing free movement with defined safeguard clauses, guaranteed preservation of the Common Travel Area with Ireland, funding to make UK systems interoperable with the EU Entry/Exit System and ETIAS, and a treaty protocol limiting the scope and timing of ECJ jurisdiction in policing and security cooperation during transition. Having led Home Office talks on preserving the Common Travel Area with Irish counterparts, they insist on a binding guarantee that CTA arrangements remain untouched throughout any transition. They co-chaired the 2019 UK-Ireland Common Travel Area MoU talks and will walk away if any draft risks forcing routine checks on the Irish land border during transition. They blocked a late draft clause in the 2019 CTA MoU talks that would have introduced ID checks on cross-border buses. After a 2017 field exercise near Newry where a trial checkpoint gridlocked the A1 and delayed cross-border school buses, they set a red line against any land-border checks during transition.

This person is a 38-year-old owner of a metal fabrication SME in the West Midlands who exports to France and Germany and wants the rejoin bid to prioritise frictionless trade: they call for rapid pre-alignment with the Union Customs Code, immediate return to CE marking instead of UKCA, joining the EU VAT One Stop Shop, and an accession roadmap that restores customs union membership and rules-of-origin relief on day one to end costly origin proofs and duplicate product conformity tests. A recent €50k shipment to Lyon sat in customs for 11 days over rules‑of‑origin queries on imported steel, wiping out our margin with penalties and rework. After EN 1090 mutual recognition ended, we paid £12k and waited six weeks to redo CE conformity for a German order. I had to take a £75k bridging loan to make payroll after the Lyon holdup. Because we source some coil from Turkey, we need diagonal cumulation or explicit rules‑of‑origin relief in any rejoin package, otherwise every EU shipment risks delays and tariffs.

This person is a 52-year-old HMRC customs IT programme manager in Essex who worries about operational risk and insists the government pair any rejoin application with a two-year dual-running plan for border systems: they want funded integration of EU tariff and classification databases (TARIC) into the UK’s CDS, a legal timetable for import VAT changes, joint UK–EU testing of ICS2/NCTS interfaces, and clear statutory guidance to avoid a cliff-edge for businesses and ports. They led parts of the CHIEF-to-CDS migration and still remember the weekend when mismatched commodity codes stranded trucks at Dover. They think the rejoin date should be tied to ICS2 Release 3 with at least six months of joint UK–EU certification to avoid another CHIEF-to-CDS–style cutover crisis. Their brother runs a small haulage firm in Thurrock, so they’ve seen how a day’s customs downtime can wipe out a week’s margins. I still keep the incident report from the CHIEF-to-CDS cutover when a faulty commodity-code update left my brother’s lorries idle for 20 hours, which is why I won’t back rejoin without a funded dual-run and a tested rollback path.

This person is a 49-year-old inshore fishing skipper from Peterhead who fears losing access if the UK re-enters the Common Fisheries Policy and therefore wants the application conditioned on a bespoke fisheries protocol: they argue for protected 12-mile limits, a renegotiated quota share based on zonal attachment, seasonal closures set by UK scientific advice, and an EU-backed compensation fund to offset any effort reductions required by a return to the CFP. If rejoining meant reverting to relative stability shares, I’d likely have to lay off my two crew. I care most about securing exclusive 12-mile access for inshore boats like mine, because over 80% of my annual catch comes from within six miles of Peterhead. In 2019 I lost two weeks’ earnings when visiting beam trawlers working the 6–12 mile band off Peterhead towed away my pots, which is why I won’t accept rejoining without a hard 12‑mile exclusion. I want any EU-backed compensation ring-fenced for low-impact gears like creels, not swallowed by offshore fleets.

This person is a 33-year-old seafood processor in Aberdeenshire whose export consignments have been delayed by post-Brexit health checks and wants rejoining sequenced to restore SPS alignment first: they propose that the UK’s application include an immediate veterinary agreement and electronic certification pilot, a guarantee of zero-tariff, zero-SPS frictions at accession, and a transition plan that keeps EU workers in processing plants through streamlined residence documentation. Last year a £20,000 consignment of chilled langoustines missed the Boulogne auction after export health certificates delayed us overnight, wiping out our profit. We lost two skilled Polish filleters over visa headaches last quarter, so streamlined residence documents for EU staff are as crucial to me as SPS alignment. Each EHC costs us about £250 and adds hours at the Boulogne SIVEP, so a Swiss-style veterinary agreement with TRACES e-cert linkage would save crucial shelf life and keep margins viable. Without a veterinary agreement and TRACES e-cert pre-notification, I’ll have to ship more frozen instead of chilled, sacrificing the 15–20% premium our French buyers pay.

This person is a 41-year-old university research grants director in Manchester who wants the application to rejoin to prioritise science and education: they advocate a negotiating sequence that immediately re-associates the UK to Horizon Europe and Erasmus+ during the accession process, restores ERC eligibility, secures GDPR adequacy to enable cross-border data sharing for research, and creates a joint committee to fast-track recognition of degrees and researcher mobility. Last year I had to pull our team out of a €6m Horizon Europe consortium and watched a rising PI relocate to Leuven to keep her ERC Starting Grant. I’m particularly anxious about the 2025 GDPR adequacy review, because if we lose it our cross-border health data projects will have to suspend EU data transfers immediately. I’m already diverting staff time to negotiate SCCs for our health datasets, and a negative adequacy decision would force an immediate, costly pause. We’ve already spent £120k this year on SCC workarounds, money I’d rather put into PhD stipends.

This person is a 68-year-old retired accountant in Doncaster on a fixed income who is open to rejoining only with strict fiscal safeguards: they demand an independent OBR-style assessment of net budget contributions, a negotiated correction mechanism akin to a rebate for the first Multiannual Financial Framework after accession, a public line-by-line account of CAP receipts versus contributions, and a binding referendum at treaty ratification so taxpayers can approve the final terms. Having kept the books for several South Yorkshire farms, they want CAP receipts broken down by region so locals can see exactly what comes back. They once had to arrange an overdraft for a South Yorkshire farm when CAP payments were delayed, so they prioritise timely, region-specific disbursements in any deal. As treasurer of a South Yorkshire farmers’ co‑op, they’ve seen CAP delays trigger overdrafts, so they want quarterly, region‑specific payment schedules with penalties for late disbursements. After a 2015 CAP delay forced their co‑op to juggle payroll with an overdraft, they now insist overdue EU farm payments accrue automatic interest earmarked for South Yorkshire claimants.

This person is a 44-year-old logistics operations manager in Belfast who manages GB–NI routes and wants rejoining to eliminate internal frictions: they argue the application must be sequenced so the entire UK re-enters the EU customs union and SPS regime simultaneously, rendering the Windsor Framework checks unnecessary, and they want guaranteed alignment of port systems and ferry schedules to avoid a new cliff-edge when the Irish Sea controls are switched off. I wrote off £18,000 of chilled stock when a Cairnryan–Larne sailing was delayed by SPS paperwork glitches, so I need a UK‑wide single‑day customs/SPS switchover with port IT and ferry schedules aligned. I’ve cobbled together brittle links between TSS, GVMS and the ferry booking portals, so I need a single integrated API live before any one‑day switchover. After losing a major supermarket contract over missed delivery windows caused by SPS holds at Larne, I can’t afford another messy, piecemeal transition. If re-entry is phased, I’d be forced to run parallel GB and EU workflows and hold duplicate safety stock, tying up six figures of working capital.

This person is a 36-year-old constitutional lawyer in Cambridge who prioritises domestic safeguards in any rejoin process: they want a detailed accession white paper, primary legislation to re-incorporate the acquis with clear parliamentary scrutiny and sunset clauses for delegated powers, explicit protocols on preliminary references to the ECJ, preservation of the Common Travel Area, and transparency over which former opt-outs (euro, Schengen, Justice and Home Affairs) the UK will seek and on what legal basis. After advising MPs on the Retained EU Law Act and witnessing sweeping Henry VIII powers in practice, they insist any rejoin bill include tight sunset clauses and robust control over delegated legislation. With an Irish partner and elderly in-laws in Cork, preserving the Common Travel Area directly affects their family's ability to travel and access care. After their Irish partner was wrongly denied boarding on a Holyhead–Dublin ferry due to confused CTA ID rules, causing a missed hospital visit in Cork, they want a statutory CTA protocol and reciprocal healthcare guarantees in the rejoin bill. Having worked on a judicial review that stalled for months over whether to seek a preliminary reference to the ECJ, they want a statutory, time‑limited protocol governing references and reasons.
